newsitem.title: UK: FOCUS - London coffee now up 40 pct this year.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - London coffee now up 40 pct this year.

text.p: London coffee futures extended a
rally on Tuesday to stand some 40 percent higher than a month ago on fears of tight world supply.
Following a lead set in the Netherlands and Germany, coffee roasters in France were the latest to decide to pass on the rise in the price of beans to the consumer in the form of higher retail prices.
A strike called by state workers in Colombia, the number two producer after Brazil, meanwhile fuelled the latest surge in coffee futures.
The benchmark May contract for Robusta coffee traded on the London Financial Futures Exchange (LIFFE) soared $80 at the opening to $1,680 per tonne before profit-taking trimmed gains slightly.
The new advance was inspired by a rally in New York on Monday where the higher quality Arabica coffee ended at a 20-month high on the March contract at 158.65 cents per pound.
The Colombian strike by some 800,000 state workers, due to start by midnight on Monday, throws yet more doubt on coffee supplies beyond concerns about expected low crops in Brazil, traders said.
"The weight of the money is on the buy side, you can't roll anything out of this market at the moment," said one trader.
London coffee prices have risen by about 40 percent since January 7 when the bellwether contract was $1,203 per tonne.
French Cafes Excella SA, a distributor brand that has a five percent market share, told Reuters that it planned to raise retail prices by 23 to 24 percent at end February-early March.
Marketing director Jean-Jacques Dothee said this meant the price of a 250 gram-pack would increase by at least two francs or about 35 US cents.

He said Arabica prices had risen sharply since December and the dollar was strong. Dothee also said that if the current rally in coffee futures continued further hikes in retail prices could not be ruled out.
"If the rise continues, we are headed for a second round of retail prices hikes in April," he said.
Industry sources said earlier Kraft Jacobs Suchard, part of the Philip Morris group, will raise French retail prices for its roasted Arabica coffees effective February 24.
Cocoa prices extended a decline on Tuesday. Traders chiefly blamed a bearish technical outlook as the London May futures price sank six pounds sterling to 876 per tonne.

Some traders wonder whether the availability of good quality cocoa is enough to justify the market's poor performance. But technical analysts described the chart picture on cocoa as overwhelmingly nervous.
Manufacturers were just buying piecemeal, watching the market go down.
Oil prices, after a long bull run, remained under pressure. But bellwether North Sea Brent crude futures traded in London little changed from Monday at around $20.90 per barrel by midday.
Gold, however, was again weaker just below $340 per ounce in a bullion market that continues haunted by fears of selling from reserves by central banks. Gold eased to a London fix of $338.85.
"Selling has re-emerged in gold. It looks like a continuation of the big sales we saw recently. It looks pretty horrible," a dealer said.
Some described the development as "quality" selling which usually refers to institutions such as central banks or producers.

Palladium reached its highest fix since May last year at $135.00 an ounce but eased later. Funds money was attracted to palladium on Monday on the back of consumer covering against delays to the start of Russian-Japanese talks on settling a 1997 supply contract.
Russia is the world's leading supplier providing over 66 percent of needs while Japan accounted for over 40 percent of demand in 1995.
Palladium is used in electronic components, autocatalysts to clean up car exhaust fumes, dentistry and a wide variety of chemical applications.
